tldr: To address the issue that single-frame or simple history inputs fail to capture environment dynamics in VLA reinforcement learning, the authors propose the World Critic Model (WCM), which jointly learns future latent state prediction and value estimation. Across 149 simulation tasks and 7 real-world robot tasks, WCM demonstrates consistently high generalization performance and success rates, not only in standard settings but also in out-of-distribution (OOD) environments.
hero_caption: An overview of the partial observability issue in conventional critics and the proposed WCM architecture. While single frames or simple history stacking fail to capture temporal progression, WCM incorporates future latent state prediction to achieve robust value estimation reflecting environment dynamics, delivering high generalization performance across both simulation and the real world.
overview:
Post-training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models using reinforcement learning (RL) has drawn significant attention. However, robotic manipulation is inherently a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). A single camera frame lacks temporal information such as object motion, contact states, and task progression.

A common intuitive idea is simply feeding past frames into the critic (value function). Yet, directly inputting high-dimensional image histories under a learning signal that merely regresses a scalar return (cumulative reward) fails to capture temporal dynamics. The critic ends up treating the history as a giant static image feature, leading to severe overfitting.

To tackle this, the authors developed the World Critic Model (WCM), which integrates a world model's prediction task directly into the critic. Built upon a lightweight LeJEPA architecture, WCM self-supervisedly predicts the next latent state from past observations while simultaneously estimating values. This naturally embeds task-relevant dynamics into the critic's internal representations.

Experiments were conducted across four benchmarks (a total of 149 tasks) including ManiSkill, MetaWorld, and CALVIN, as well as 7 real-world tasks on a WidowX robot arm. WCM substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating remarkable strength in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization when objects and backgrounds change.
contributions: Identified the representation bottleneck in VLA-RL critics, uncovering the root cause of why single-frame or naive history inputs fail to recover temporal structure under POMDPs
Proposed the World Critic Model (WCM), a lightweight critic architecture that end-to-end integrates future latent state prediction with value estimation to explicitly learn environmental dynamics
Demonstrated high flexibility by seamlessly applying WCM across representative VLA models such as OpenVLA-OFT, π₀, and π₀.₅ in both on-policy and off-policy pipelines
Showed consistent state-of-the-art performance across 149 simulation tasks and 7 real-world tasks, achieving major gains not only in-distribution (IND) but also out-of-distribution (OOD)

sections.heading: Why Couldn't Conventional Critics Understand "Time"?
sections.summary: Because robotic manipulation is a POMDP, single frames miss critical dynamic information like contact and velocity. However, naively feeding past frames to the critic causes overfitting, as scalar return regression alone cannot learn temporal changes. To break this representation bottleneck, the authors conceived WCM to actively predict future latent states.
sections.details:
Post-training pretrained VLA models using reinforcement learning (RL) is rapidly emerging as a way to surpass the limitations of imitation learning (supervised fine-tuning, SFT). In critic-based RL in particular, the critic supplies dense gradients and weights for policy updates; thus, its estimation accuracy heavily dictates sample efficiency and final performance.

However, robot manipulation is a quintessential POMDP (Partially Observable Markov Decision Process). A single static image only captures appearance and object placement, omitting dynamic information like velocity, acceleration, and the progression of contact. According to POMDP theory, optimal decision-making requires sufficient statistics of the observation history. Despite this, most existing VLA-RL frameworks still regress values from single-frame visual inputs or single-frame VLM features.

Does stacking past frames (frame stacking) solve the issue? It is not that simple. When stacking past frames in a high-dimensional visual space, the learning signal—a scalar return per step—is far too weak. As a result, instead of learning dynamic transition rules, the critic simply memorizes past frames as massive static features.

This is where the authors found their breakthrough. Just as language models acquire rich internal representations via next-token prediction, why not task the critic with predicting future latent states? By doing so, explicit dynamics are incorporated into the critic's latent representation, enabling more accurate and generalizable value estimation.

sections.heading: Historical Challenges in VLA Reinforcement Learning and Critics
sections.summary: The paper surveys RL methods for recent VLA models, including autoregressive and flow-matching types. While policies increasingly leverage histories, critics have remained dependent on single frames. WCM draws inspiration from world models (such as WAM) to address these representation challenges in high-dimensional visual space.
sections.details:
Recent VLA models broadly fall into two families: autoregressive (AR) models that generate tokens sequentially like LLMs (such as OpenVLA), and flow-matching models that solve continuous probability flows (such as π₀). Both have shown improved generalization and robustness through RL fine-tuning after SFT.

However, the critic models underpinning this RL have faced long-standing challenges. Conventional methods rely on regressing values from a single frame, which inherently creates an information deficit in POMDP settings. While some studies began introducing observation history on the policy side, no definitive method existed for the critic to exploit history effectively. The massive input space and the sparse scalar return signal prevented models from capturing relationships across frames.

Meanwhile, approaches that use prediction error as a representation learning signal, such as World Models or World Action Models (WAM) which jointly output actions and predictions, have gained prominence. This study positions WCM to introduce this powerful world model prediction objective into critic representation learning, fundamentally preventing the limitations and overfitting of single-frame regression.

sections.heading: WCM Architecture: Integrating Future Prediction with Value Estimation
sections.summary: Formulated as a POMDP, WCM is proposed based on the lightweight self-supervised LeJEPA architecture. From historical features generated by encoders, a Causal Transformer simultaneously predicts future latent states and state values. With SIGReg regularization to prevent feature collapse, it is designed for both on-policy and off-policy pipelines.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
Robotic manipulation is formulated as a POMDP $(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{R},\gamma)$. The agent cannot directly observe the true hidden state $s_t$; it only receives partial observations $o_t$ (images, joint states, language instructions) and aims to maximize the expected cumulative discounted return.

### 3.2 Structure and Objectives of the World Critic Model
WCM is designed around the LeJEPA architecture to allow lightweight training even from scratch. It consists of four primary components:
- **Observation Encoder**: Independently embeds the past $K$ image frames into latent representations (using a ViT or VLM backbone).
- **Language Adapter**: Projects the language instruction $\ell$ extracted via CLIP into the latent space.
- **World Predictor**: A Causal Transformer that takes language tokens and visual history as input, outputting a latent representation $h_t$ of the entire history.
- **Two Decoder Heads**: A value decoder that outputs a scalar value $\hat{V}_t$ from $h_t$, and a world prediction decoder that predicts the next latent state $\hat{z}_{t+1}$ in a residual form conditioned on the current action $a_t$.

The training loss is the sum of three terms:
1. **Prediction Loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}$**: The L2 error between the predicted next state $\hat{z}_{t+1}$ and the actual true next state $z_{t+1}$ (computed using teacher-forcing).
2. **Regularization Loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{SIGReg}}$**: A regularizer that aligns randomly projected distributions with an isotropic Gaussian to prevent dimensional collapse in latent representations.
3. **Value Loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{value}}$**: The L2 error between the normalized return $G_t$ and the predicted value $\hat{V}_t$.
Overall, the model minimizes $\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{value}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}} + \eta \mathcal{L}_{\text{SIGReg}}$ end-to-end.

### 3.3 Training Pipelines
In on-policy settings, WCM uses PPO for OpenVLA-OFT and Flow-SDE for π₀/π₀.₅, updating policies with Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) computed from WCM values. To save computational costs, the VLM backbone is reused as the encoder.
In off-policy settings, teleoperated SFT demonstrations are mixed with RL rollouts (both successes and failures) in a replay buffer, training AR models with AWR and flow models with RECAP.

sections.heading: Thorough Validation Across 149 Simulation and 7 Real-World Tasks
sections.summary: Evaluated across four benchmarks—ManiSkill, MetaWorld, CALVIN, and LIBERO-Plus—WCM achieves SOTA across all settings. It demonstrates dramatic improvements from zero-shot initializations and superior OOD generalization. On 7 real-world WidowX tasks, it also clearly outperforms baseline methods in success rate.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Simulation experiments spanned 149 tasks across ManiSkill (in-distribution and perturbed out-of-distribution OOD), MetaWorld (diverse contact-rich tasks), CALVIN (long-horizon sequential tasks), and LIBERO-Plus (generalization evaluation). Baselines included Flow-Noise, Flow-SDE, π-StepNFT, PPO, and GRPO.
Real-world experiments utilized a WidowX-250S robot arm across 7 tasks trained via off-policy RL: catching moving sushi (dynamic grasping), cloth and towel folding (deformable objects), stove cleaning (long-horizon), and vegetable pick-and-place.

### 4.2 Key Simulation Results
- **ManiSkill**: Substantial gains over SFT baselines. OpenVLA-OFT achieved a 252% performance improvement. Starting from a near-zero initial state without ManiSkill pretraining (0.78% success rate), WCM-powered RL reliably scaled performance up by 12,551% (close to 100%).
- **MetaWorld & CALVIN**: Consistently surpassed baselines in MetaWorld, which requires stable contact, and CALVIN, which entails long-horizon sequences. This confirms that the critic accurately captures dynamic higher-order states under POMDP conditions.

### 4.3 Out-of-Distribution Generalization (OOD)
Compared to π-StepNFT, known for its robustness to perturbations, WCM achieved higher success rates on ManiSkill OOD evaluations. In LIBERO-Plus, starting from a One-SFT model trained on only a single demonstration, WCM with just 250 RL steps outperformed the Full-SFT baseline trained on 50 demonstrations (20,000 trajectories total), showing dramatic generalization capabilities.

### 4.4 Real-World Results
On the real robot, a WCM with 107.2M trainable parameters was deployed. Starting from 100 SFT trajectories per task, training ran for 8 RL iterations (50 rollouts per iteration, totaling hundreds to thousands of samples, taking under 1 hour of training). Compared to a Gemma 270M critic baseline, WCM achieved higher success rates and smoother motions across all 7 tasks, including dynamic sushi catching and soft cloth folding.

sections.heading: Ablations Reveal the Value of World Prediction and the Optimal History Length
sections.summary: Comparing against ViT and MLP critics without the world prediction loss ($\lambda=0$) proves that the predictive objective itself is essential for utilizing history. Furthermore, a history length of 3 frames was found to be optimal, fully capturing kinematic dynamics such as velocity and acceleration without redundancy.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Is the World Prediction Objective Truly Necessary?
Is the performance boost simply due to feeding history images into the critic? To verify this, the authors compared critic architectures across three models: π₀, π₀.₅, and OpenVLA-OFT.
- **MLP Critic (Baseline)**: Increasing the number of history frames actually led to degraded performance.
- **ViT Critic (WCM with $\lambda=0$)**: Despite having temporal attention, performance barely improved with more history frames when world prediction was absent.
- **WCM (Proposed)**: Incorporating the future prediction loss unlocked substantial performance gains, fully leveraging the benefits of history.
This demonstrates that simply "inputting history" is insufficient; forcing the model to "learn dynamics by predicting the future" is the crucial factor.

### 5.2 Is Longer History Always Better?
Varying the history length $K$ from 1 to 5 showed that an average length of 3 frames achieved the highest performance. Physically, 2 frames capture velocity (first-order difference) and 3 frames capture acceleration (second-order difference). These first- and second-order dynamics appear sufficient to represent the physics required for manipulation; extending history further introduces redundancy and overfitting that outweigh the benefits.

sections.heading: Deep Dive from the Appendix: Overfitting Suppression and Sim-to-Real Insights
sections.summary: The appendix provides sensitivity analysis for the loss weight $\lambda$, the impact of the critic on policy generalization, value curve visualisations, and intriguing Sim-to-Real findings. It confirms that WCM avoids extreme outliers under OOD conditions and maintains stable value landscapes.
sections.details:
### Impact of Loss Weight $\lambda$
Varying the world prediction weight $\lambda$ showed that intermediate values in $[0.3, 0.5]$ yielded the best results for both IND and OOD. Setting a stronger prediction weight ($\lambda=0.9$) resulted in higher OOD performance than prioritizing value regression ($\lambda=0.1$), confirming that world prediction actively aids generalization.

### Critic Overfitting and OOD Performance
In conventional Flow-SDE, a "dropping phenomenon" (overfitting) was observed where OOD performance degraded as training progressed. In contrast, an ablation completely removing the critic mitigated this drop, suggesting that scalar value regression in the critic is the primary cause of overfitting. WCM strongly suppressed this degradation, maintaining high generalization even after 500 steps. 2D workspace value heatmaps also showed that while baselines produced extreme anomalous values in unseen regions, WCM generated smooth, discriminative value landscapes.

### Value Curve Visualizations
On successful simulation trajectories, WCM's predicted values increased monotonically toward the goal. On failure trajectories (random actions or misalignments), predicted values dropped sharply after task onset or collapsed after an initial rise, correctly diagnosing task success and failure.

### Surprising Sim-to-Real Findings
A model trained on 16,800 simulation trajectories via SFT failed to complete a single grasp when deployed directly to the real robot. However, fine-tuning with SFT on just 50 real-world samples followed by simulation RL caused grasping success rates on unseen objects (such as bananas and bell peppers) to jump dramatically. Reward-maximizing exploration in simulation RL is hypothesized to break narrow environment memorization, encouraging the acquisition of generalizable grasping features.

takeaways: Merely feeding observation history into a robot RL critic is insufficient; dynamics are truly reflected in representations only when coupled with a future prediction objective
For dynamic robot manipulation tasks, an input history length of 3 frames serves as a practical sweet spot covering both velocity and acceleration
Critic overfitting to scalar returns is a major factor deteriorating overall policy generalization (OOD), making world model regularization a key driver for generalization
WCM offers a versatile architecture that seamlessly integrates into both autoregressive and flow-matching VLA models, across both on-policy and off-policy training pipelines
limitations: When history length exceeds 3 frames, computational attention costs increase while performance plateaus, requiring different mechanisms to capture very long-term dependencies

In on-policy pipelines, the VLM backbone's latent space is directly used, omitting the SIGReg collapse regularizer due to computational constraints, which presents a trade-off with theoretical completeness
A significant sim-to-real gap remains, meaning zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without real data remains unresolved
